utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. I imagine it feels like yesterday to you all when we last met. However, a bit of time has elapsed and one or two issues have arisen during that period that should be addressed before we proceed any further today. I'm going to deal with two administrative matters first of all. The final request that the Prosecution made for admission of documents from the bar table, the third request, involved the absence at that time of translations of certain of the documents. Time was allowed for the production of these translations until today. The Prosecution seek a further two days, that's until Wednesday of this week, to provide the absent translations. Obviously, if that motion follows its ordinary course, the time will have elapsed before it could possibly be dealt with. It would be helpful to us to know if there is to be any opposition to that motion. I take the silence as an indication that there is no opposition to it. The Chamber will therefore grant the motion. The second matter is the -- or does relate to evidence today and I suppose is not really a preliminary matter, so I'll deal with it in the context of looking at where we are in the conduct of the Prosecution case. The -- it was initially anticipated that today we would know the outcome of the Prosecution appeal in relation to the evidence of General Clark; however, that decision has not yet been taken. Whatever that decision would have been, it was also open to the Prosecution to call certain other evidence today, and I gather that available is a witness, Shaun Byrnes, that the Prosecution intend to lead. However, related to that is the other administrative matter I want to raise and that is that there is a letter from Messrs. Lukic and Ivetic for the accused Lukic which was sent to the government of the Rule 70 witness, seeking authority to cross-examine him on certain matters which go beyond the terms of the authorised examination -- or the limited examination-in-chief. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I'm getting an indication from the US representatives that they have not seen that letter. Can you tell me what date it was sent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's dated the 12th of April. Mr. Ivetic will tell us where exactly it was sent. My copy is addressed to the headquarters, but it may be that copies were sent to the office in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that the letter was presented to the Registry and it was via the Registry of the Tribunal delivered to the State Department. That's what I was told, since there was some concern as to which particular office or official would be the appropriate one for that. It's my understanding that Ms. Delic and other officials of the Registry were in contact with my colleagues and that the letter was sent through the Registry to the appropriate individuals at the State Department. So I presume that would be the ones here in The Hague, but I really cannot say with certainty that it would be the ones here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The copy I have seen does say that it's a courtesy copy, so let's briefly or quickly check what the official position is. That -- it's not possible to clarify the position as quickly as we would like. It will be clarified as soon as possible. If there is no difficulty about the transmission of the communication itself, then arrangements will be made to ensure that copies are distributed while we are sitting here, in the hope that the issues can be quickly reviewed. It may not be easy to get a clear answer to all of them; but even if some were answered fairly quickly, it would help progress matters. I think that's all we can ask in the circumstances. Mr. Hannis, do you have any other preliminary issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We are ready to call Mr. Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anyone, any Defence counsel, who has any other preliminary issue? All right. When Mr. Philips gave evidence, there seemed to be a degree of confusion about the exact role of the representatives of the provider government in court. For the avoidance of doubt, I would like to explain that we see their role as twofold: Either -- in fact, both might apply depending on the particular issue. But their role is either to alert you, the Prosecution to a situation where it's felt that there should be a decision made not to allow a question, for example, or to intervene in some respect. So we recognise that that may be an appropriate way of relaying their concerns to the Bench. But equally, we would recognise their direct intervention if it is felt that that is necessary and appropriate, and that's a matter for their judgement; but between you, I hope we can avoid the apparent uncertainty there was the last time. Just bear in mind it is open to you to raise matters either through the Prosecution or directly yourselves where that seems necessary, and I stress necessary and appropriate. Obviously, it's more satisfactory if it's always dealt with through the Prosecutor, but we do not insist on that as a restriction that should apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I appreciate that guidance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have just remembered one other matter I should have dealt with earlier. Mr. Byrnes could you have a seat for a moment? We are dealing with one or two administrative -- and there is one that I should have raised also. Mr. Hannis, you have raised the issue over the possibility of another witness, in addition to Mr. Byrnes, but one who is not available today, and you ask that we reconsider the initial indication we gave that that witness -- well, in the event that your appeal is unsuccessful, that witness ought to be available immediately the Trial Chamber sits again after the decision. I take it that's been intimated to the Defence, that application.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, is there to be a response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We received notification that the Prosecution would make an oral application, and we are prepared to make an oral response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So should we deal with that when we have to deal with it; in other words at the end of the evidence of the present witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for the Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's the best plan. Let's see where we get to and deal with the matter at that stage. I'm sorry about that, Mr. Byrnes. Could you stand now, please? And would you make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which you now have in your hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This is a witness, Your Honour, that we've called pursuant to Rule 70, and the conditions that have been ordered pursuant to our application is that his direct examination will be limited to the supplemental 65 ter summary that we filed, that cross-examination will be likewise limited to the scope of that examination-in-chief, and matters affecting his credibility, and any others that the Rule 70 provider might agree to later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, could you state your name for the record, please, and would you spell it for us?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My name is Shaun Michael Byrnes, and it is spelled in American English, S-H-A-U-N, Michael, M-I-C-H-A-E-L. Byrnes is spelled B-Y-R-N-E-S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes, and you're doing a good job of it so far. Since we both speak English, it's important for the translators and the interpreters if we give a pause between my question and your answer likewise. Sir, I understand you're currently retired?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm happily retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what kind of work did you do before you retired? What was your profession?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I spent nearly 30 years as an officer in the United States foreign service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998, did you become involved in a mission that was known by the acronym KDOM, K-D-O-M?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what KDOM stands for?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The initials "KDOM" stand for Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about how that came into existence, and how you became connected with it?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission came into being as a result of an agreement that I understand was reached in Moscow in mid-June of 1998. The agreement was between the president of what we call ex-Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, and the then-president of the Russian republic, Boris Yeltsin. The agreement was intended to try to, as I understand, to try to stabilise the situation in Kosovo which had become increasingly violent, in the spring of 1998. Under the agreement, Mr. Milosevic agreed that diplomatic representatives would have full powers to monitor and observe what was occurring then in Kosovo. The hope was that greater international observation would lead to a calming down of the situations, to permit time for a political solution to be found. Ambassador Dick Holbrooke came -- let me back up a little bit. Violence continued through June so much so that Ambassador Holbrooke was sent to Belgrade to discuss the situation with President Milosevic. As a result of those discussions, it was agreed that an international observer mission would be established and that is how KDOM came into being. Let me add one additional fact which I think is -- may be important for subsequent discussion today. KDOM was the general acronym, Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission; however, the agreement was that there would actually be three international observer missions. One which would be staffed by the Russian republic, and colloquially in Kosovo became known as Russian KDOM. A second would be under the aegis of the European Union. It became known as EU KDOM, and the third diplomatic mission was the American one, which was called US KDOM. To answer the second part of your question, I was the political minister, counsellor, in Rome. At the time, I had extensive experience in Yugoslavia. I had served in our embassy in Belgrade from 1980 to 1984. I had also been sent back to Belgrade in 1992 for three months to help out. Our embassy was under staffed at the time and conflict in Bosnia and Croatia was growing. The Department of State wanted somebody who knew something about Yugoslavia, and I was close. I had the proper rank. I spoke some Serbian, and I did know something about Kosovo because in the 1980s, one of my portfolios as political officer in the political section of our embassy in Belgrade was to follow events in Kosovo which, as I think all of you know, had become somewhat troubled after the demonstrations and riots of March 1981. So they asked me to do it. I agreed to do it. The original agreement was I would go for six weeks and set the mission up and come back and the rest is history.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So when did you start with U.S. KDOM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I arrived in Belgrade from Rome on August 10th of 1998. I arrived in Pristina to take over US KDOM, which had been initially stood up at the very end of July and had an acting chief, an US army lieutenant-colonel. In any case, I arrived in Pristina on August the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say you were originally supposed to go for six weeks, but I take it from your answer you ended up staying much longer?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you eventually leave?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I left Kosovo finally at the end of July of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you in Kosovo between the 23rd of March and mid-June?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No, sir, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that later. Who was your immediate boss when you were acting as head of US KDOM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: US KDOM -- let me start over again. We had bilateral relations with Yugoslavia, with Belgrade. So when Department of State agreed to establish US KDOM, it was established as an entity of the US embassy in Belgrade. So I reported directly to our chief of mission, Ambassador Richard Miles, our chief of mission in Belgrade, and that embassy provided us with full administrative support; and on matters of policy and substance, I took directions from Dick Miles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were you physically stationed or your primary base?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: US KDOM was established in a motel owned by a pair of Kosovo Serbs that was located in a suburb of Pristina. The suburb was called Kosovo Polje. If I recall, it was about six kilometres to the west of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was your mandate? What was your assignment as head of US KDOM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: As the title of the mission suggests, our primary mission was to observe what was occurring in Kosovo at the time. I think Holbrooke and others who had agreed to the establishment of these missions felt that one, they were not getting accurate information from about what was occurring in Kosovo prior to the KDOM, the three KDOMs establishment. They weren't getting accurate information from either side or even from the international press which had begun to become interested. Both sides were manipulating, I think, the press. That was the sort of sense. So in the first place, if the international community and Belgrade were to have any hope of finding a political solution to the Kosovo problem, they required accurate information as to what was in fact going on. So that was our primary mission. There was also, I think, there was a hope expressed to me that an intrusive international presence on the ground would help calm things down and reduce conflict. And at the end of the day from my standpoint, and I can say this sentiment was shared by every single member of my mission, at the end of the day, we would -- we would save lives. We would save Serbian lives, and we would save Albanian lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Hannis, can I ask one question? I've lost one link, I think, along the way in what you said, Mr. Byrnes, about the establishment of KDOM. My initial impression was that these missions were established as the result of the agreement reached in Moscow, and then you backed up and told us that violence continued through June and Holbrooke was sent and following his visit, there was agreement on these diplomatic missions. Now, was the setting up of these missions a two-stage process or have I perhaps separated the thing into too many parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the lack of clarity, Your Honour, in my presentation. The problem is mine. I'll try to be clearer this time. What President Milosevic and President Yeltsin agreed in June in Moscow was the principle, and that principle was that the diplomatic missions in Belgrade would have greater access and would be indeed encouraged to monitor the situation and collect information about what was occurring in Kosovo. Second, so to be very clear, Your Honour, there was no agreement to establish formal diplomatic observer missions. Dick Holbrooke, when he went, the violence as I said persisted. Holbrooke then went to Belgrade in an effort to try to calm things down and find a solution. Holbrooke seized on the language in the memorandum or the letter, I can't remember exactly what it was, that both President Milosevic and President Yeltsin signed in June. He seized on the language providing for more extensive diplomatic monitoring, obviously foreign diplomatic monitoring of Kosovo, to propose the establishment of specific missions. This would no longer -- the observation would no longer be left to diplomatic missions in Belgrade. There would be established formal missions, formal observer missions in Pristina to carry out that task, and President Milosevic agreed to that. I hope that clarifies that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were three KDOMs then. There was US, EU, and the Russian KDOM. Can you tell us roughly what were the differences in terms of numbers between those three? Which was the biggest?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Initially, European Union KDOM was the biggest because European Commission had a monitoring mission in Kosovo which they simply renamed EU KDOM, and they had something, I don't recall the exact numbers, but they had something like 12 or 15 officers already in Kosovo and they had been there since April of 1998. However, our mission was established in late July and quickly became larger than the European Union's mission. The Russian mission was established somewhat later. As I recall, it was established in early September and the Russian mission never became very large. I think, at the maximum, the Russians had five or six officers, and they had no four-wheel-drive or even armoured vehicles which would permit them to go off road outside of Pristina. The Russians -- the Russian mission, I think, did not become very large, very simply because Moscow had resource problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And eventually how big did the EU and US KDOMs come to be, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Six or seven or eight years later, my memory is not the sharpest, but the US mission in late December or early January -- late December 1998, early January 1999, numbered, I recall, in the neighbourhood of 300 US officers and 600 or 700 Albanian and Serbian local national employees. The European Union mission, I think, at one point had something like 37 officers. Let me just add, if I may, that that mission was made up of a wide range of representatives of the European Union. It was headed by a British officer but it had Italians, Germans, Slovaks, Frenchmen, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What were your duties in KDOM? What -- you told us that you were set up to observe. How did you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: From the very beginning, we ran what we called missions. We initially had three or four armoured Chevrolet Suburbans, four wheel drive off road vehicles. And we would send them out in the morning with a team that consisted of at least three people; one of those was a local national interpreter, either a Serb or an Albanian. In each instance that local national, regardless of his or her nationality, had to speak both languages; the Serb had to speak Albanian, the Albanian had to speak Serbian. There were plenty of Serbs, of course, that did speak good Albanian. In any case, these -- we would direct these vehicles and these missions into areas that were contested or which we knew there were on going confrontations or clashes or there were humanitarian problems. They would spend the day in those areas, observing, talking to people of both nationalities. Let me add, too, that because we had resource limitations, particularly at the outset, and EU KDOM did as well. And there was a lot of ground to cover. We coordinated very closely with the EU KDOM. The EU KDOM chief and I met every evening and exchanged reports, our mission reports. They knew what our people had seen and reported, and we knew what their people had seen and reported. And we then discussed where we should send vehicles the next day, what appeared to be potential hot spots, the flash points; and then we would take and look what are the resources the two of us had, and we would just divide up areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You answered what was going to be my next question. How about the Russians? How did they figure in this, even though there were maybe only half dozen of them?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: As soon as the Russian mission was set up, we made arrangements to - we being the United States KDOM and the EU KDOM - we made arrangements to take Russian officers along on our missions. As I said earlier, the Russians lacked off-the-road vehicles and they lacked armoured vehicles, and I would add that the Russian KDOM chief, who was Sergei Lavrov, not to be confused with the present Foreign Minister, had what I considered legitimate concerns about the security of Russian missions off the road in areas where there was a lot of KLA activity. And they simply didn't want to go there, but they would go there with us. They had an obligation to report to Moscow. I would add, if I may, that we found -- first, we worked very closely with the Russians. We had an obligation to provide a weekly report to the Contact Group ambassadors in Belgrade and that report was drawn up together by myself, the EU KDOM chief, and the Russian KDOM chief. The Russians were very, very good. The Russians were cooperative. The Russians worked closely with us. We never had any problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In light of what had been happening before you started on your mission, did you have some concerns about just hopping in your vehicles and driving around Kosovo? Did you make any arrangements with local authorities to figure out where you were going to go and when you were going to go? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My recollection is that we did not inform the Serbian police of our planned missions; however, we did work closely with them. I think it's important to add here that we had no contact with the Yugoslav army in Pristina. We, of course, would -- our missions would encounter the Yugoslav military in the field on occasion, but there was no official contact. We did have official contact with the Serbian police, but we didn't share our mission plans with them, I think, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the course of carrying out your mission, did you have dealings with any political authorities in Kosovo or in Serbia, Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who did you deal with?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: See, I dealt -- on the Serbian side, I dealt primarily with the prefect of Pristina Opstina, Pristina County, a man named Veljko Odalovic. I met Mr. Odalovic, I think, the second day I arrived in Pristina. Ambassador Miles took me to Mr. Odalovic office to introduce us. It was important that we work closely with them. KDOM was there to assist both parties, to try to make the situation better; and to achieve that goal, we had to work with the local political authorities. So I had a good deal of contact with Mr. Odalovic in Pristina. Our teams had contact with local Serb officials in the field; and in Belgrade, Ambassador Miles at one point introduced me to Nikola Sainovic who was a Deputy Prime Minister, first Deputy Prime Minister, and who Ambassador Miles considered to have the Kosovo, if you will, the Kosovo portfolio in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what Ambassador Miles told you?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To be perfectly frank, I do not remember exactly. That was certainly my -- my present impression is, that I understood at the time, was that Mr. Sainovic was, if you will, the go-to, the point man politically on Kosovo. And whether Ambassador Miles told me that, I can't remember. Whether Mr. Sainovic told me that when I was introduced to them, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have subsequent dealings with Mr. Sainovic after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How often or how many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Sainovic on, I would say, a number of occasions. I had a fair amount of dealings with him. They usually -- my recollection is that they were always linked with a -- one or another of the continuing crises that we had to deal with in Kosovo. I dealt with him in Belgrade when I was there, and I dealt with him in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And those subsequent dealings you had with him, were they consistent with the way Miles had presented him to you as being the point man for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that the number of occasions you had contact with him seemed to be crisis-related. Can you give us an example of what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The crisis that most immediately comes to mind was the one with one, for example, in early January, when eight Yugoslav army soldiers misread a map on a patrol, in an area of Kosovo, a hilly, rough area in Kosovo north of Kosovska Mitrovica, and they stumbled into a UCK encampment of some sort and were captured. It was obviously very important for Belgrade to get these soldiers back and very important for us - by us, I mean the international community - to get these soldiers back and resolve a crisis. Any time something like this happened, there was a great fear that there would be renewed fighting across the province, and in which case our diplomacy would have completely failed. I worked -- I recall that I worked very closely with Mr. Sainovic to find a resolution to this crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've heard other evidence about this but were you successful?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, we were. Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to back up for a minute. You mentioned earlier that you speak some Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you speak any Albanian?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any other languages?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I speak Russian and Croatian and Italian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how good would you characterise your Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My Serbian, then, when I got there, was pretty rusty. I hadn't used it in six or seven years. It got considerably better because I used it over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, you said earlier that you didn't have any contact with a VJ representative in Pristina. How about with the MUP, the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I had quite a bit of contact with the MUP, particularly with General Sreten Lukic at the time. It was part of my, if you will, work requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you first get introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I recall that I was introduced to General Lukic on August the 13th. I was taken to his office by Ambassador Miles is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how often did you have dealings with him during your time in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I had many, many, many dealings with General Lukic, particularly in the period up to and immediately after the establishment of the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission in late October or early November. After OSCE - we called it KVM for shorthand - after the establishment of the KVM, responsibility for dealing with the Serbian police, with the Serbian authorities, on questions related to our mission passed from the KDOMs to the new OSCE, Kosovo Verification Mission headed by Ambassador William Walker, but I still had contact with General Lukic afterwards, often in situations that were crisis-related.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the time period when you first started in August until KVM got started up, were you seeing him on a weekly basis, a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I often saw General Lukic on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the nature of your daily contacts with him? What did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The discussions centred on what was taking place in Kosovo. I often brought to his attention the observations of our teams in the field, observations of what we considered unacceptable or unacceptable behaviour on the part of the Serbian police; for example, the burning of villages and destruction of personal property that our teams had observed on the spot. He, on his part, would often call me, call me in, to complain of the activities of the Kosovo -- the KLA, the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what would you do when you got informed by him about KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Our obligation was to check those out. We could not do our job if we did not, and we would -- depending on the allegation, it might involve violence of some sort in a part of Kosovo. We could try to send a team there to verify the report. Most often, what sticks out in my memory - and let me stress for the Court that my memory, after close to nine years, my memory of these events is certainly fuzzy - but what does stick in my mind is either the killing or the disappearance of Serbs. Whenever -- whenever this happened, General Lukic would be on the phone to me asking for our help in trying to ascertain what had happened and, of course, most importantly to try to find these people and get them back. And we did -- we did honestly everything we possibly could. And fortunately we were successful on some occasions, and unfortunately those occasions were far too few.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us before about your dealings with Mr. Sainovic. Did you ever meet Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Milutinovic -- when I was there, Mr. Milutinovic was president of Serbia. I met him formally on two occasions, both were centred on the negotiations in Belgrade in late October that produced the so-called October agreement. And I saw him -- I saw him at Rambouillet as a member of the Serbian delegation. I never had any conversations or any dealings with him, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regard to the VJ, even though you didn't have any liaison or contact in Pristina, did you have any dealings with high-ranking officers in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, what do you mean by "dealings"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet and speak with them? For example, did you ever meet General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I never met General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, sir, I never met General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I recall meeting General Pavkovic on only one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That occasion was in Pristina shortly after -- if my memory is correct, it was shortly after the October agreement. General Pavkovic summoned the KDOM officials to a meeting in his offices at Pristina corps command centre in the centre of town, to go over based on what we Americans would call the rules-of-the-road; reviewing the agreement, what his obligations to us were, and what our duties were. That sort of thing. Just as a footnote, October agreement established KVM, the OSCE mission, but the KDOMs stood in for KVM until it was stood up and operational. So we were the ones who went to this meeting. It was a very professional meeting. I recall there were probably 30 people around the table. General Pavkovic was very professional, very direct, and that was -- I don't believe I ever saw him again or ever had contact with him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During your tour of duty as head of KDOM when you -- well, did you go out in the field yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I did indeed. I tried to go into the field at least twice a week. I felt that -- I felt that I could not deal with, particularly, I could not deal with the Serbian leadership in Pristina, General Lukic or Mr. Odalovic. I could not report accurately to Washington through our Ambassador in Belgrade, Richard Miles. I could not report to the Contact Group Ambassadors who periodically came down, unless I had some experience of the field. I had some feel for what was transpiring there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of going out into the field to observe, did you have occasion to speak with any VJ officers about the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about any of those discussions and any particular individuals you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I had a couple of discussions when we would run into VJ units. The discussions were always professional and always brief. My recollection is we dealt with middle-grade officers, senior lieutenants, captains, who were, I would say, professional in their conduct to us, with us, and very reticent about what they were doing or why they were there and the size of the units, that sort of thing. That, I considered, a professional response, and I would add that -- I would add two things. One, on one occasion, I don't remember where or when, and I certainly don't have a name. These officers would not provide that information, which was their right. On one occasion, a junior officer hinted to me, since I spoke some Serbian, that he wasn't particularly pleased to be there and doing what he was doing, but it was only a hint and he did not go beyond that. The other thing I would like to say is, about the VJ in the field, was they were -- they were helpful in their contacts with us. In our judgement, when they gave us advice about particular places to go and not to go, it was given to us in good faith. Our sense of the VJ was they had no desire to see us get hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the MUP for a minute. You mentioned your dealings with General Lukic. Did you meet any other generals or high-ranking members of the MUP in the course of your tour with the KDOM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you meet General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When and how and what was the nature of that contact?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I met General Djordjevic on at least two occasions. The occasion that I have the clearest recollection of was in, I think, 24, 25 October, 1998, in Belgrade, on the occasion of the talks that General Clark and General Naumann from NATO came down to conduct and which led to the so-called Belgrade agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. I met General Djordjevic on one other occasion in Pristina. It was very brief, and to be perfectly honest, I have no recollection of the substance of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Obrad Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I had contact with General Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What can you recall about that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I saw General Stefanovic both in Pristina and in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was your understanding about his relationship vis-a-vis General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What I recollect is that when I arrived in Kosovo, and when I first met General Lukic, my recollection is that he or somebody told me that he, General Lukic, was replacing General Stefanovic as the Serbian police chief in Kosovo; secondly, that General Lukic reported to Belgrade, to General Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was your understanding about the position of General Djordjevic vis-a-vis Stefanovic and Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Well, General Djordjevic was head of the -- that part of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that was responsible for public order, so he was -- he was, if you will, General Stefanovic's and General Lukic's boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you meet General Lukic's deputy in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. I worked with Colonel - I can't remember his first name - but his last name was Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often did you have dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I had quite a few dealings with Colonel Mijatovic over time, in part because General Lukic went to Belgrade once a week and Mijatovic would step in and replace him; and then I recall that there was one period of a week or so when General Lukic became, I understand, was quite ill and stayed in Belgrade, and so Mijatovic was his replacement. The other thing I remember about that relationship was that after the October agreement, KDOMs were asked to try to see if we could work out what I would call two cease fires in two places. They had been traditionally very hot. One was the Malisevo area in central Kosovo and the other was the area around Podujevo. I worked very closely with Colonel Mijatvic in trying to accomplish something in the Malisevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you work with anybody on political side in connection with that Malisevo effort?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Sir, to be honest, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware of, in addition to just the regular police that were part of the Ministry of the Interior, were you aware of any other units or components of the MUP that you saw present in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. The -- what were called the special police, the PJP, were very, very much in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did they differ from what I would refer to as the normal or regular police?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: There was a substantial difference, certainly organisationally and structurally. The PJP were an organised light infantry. Basically, it was an organised light infantry unit made up of young, fit, if you will, soldiers or policemen. The PJP units were equipped with what I would call light infantry weapons. They had -- and we saw this. We saw this in the field. I saw this in the field. I'm not reporting simply what my teams reported. They were equipped with automatic rifles; light, certainly light machine-guns; they had light armoured vehicles; scout cars; armoured personnel carriers. They were effectively light infantry. If I may, because I spent a great deal of my career in the Soviet Union, I would compare them to the internal security troops that were organised and operated under the Ministry of -- the Soviet Ministry of Internal Affairs. The PJP was clearly an organised light infantry unit that could backstop police in a situation where perhaps you had an insurgency or something like that, but these were not your policemen who walked a beat in a city or drove patrol cars in Belgrade or Novi Sad. They were to respond, if you will, to crises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said in part of your answer that you personally observed the PJP in operations in the field in Kosovo. Can you tell us approximately when and where that was?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I cannot frankly give you a date. I don't remember the date, but I can still see the scene in my mind's eye. It was very good weather. There were still crops in the field. What I saw probably occurred in mid-or late September of 1998. I had chosen to go with a mission that day that was going into an area where there had been a good deal of trouble, and we turned south. We went west on the road from Pristina towards Pec and Kijevo, which was a mixed Serbian-Albanian village. We turned south towards Malisevo. And in the village, some several kilometres south of Kijevo - and I don't remember the name of the village unfortunately - we arrived as the village was being torched. There were blue police buses and armoured cars and scout vehicles there; police blue. They were not VJ, I'd like to stress. And I watched as a number of these PJP officers, with their weapons, boarded the buses and prepared to drive off. My team and I also watched PJP officers emerging from the alley ways in the village. I need to stress this is what I saw. I did not see a single PJP officer pull a trigger. I did not see a PJP officer light a house on fire by whatever means, but there were no Albanians. There were no Albanians about. They had fled and the village was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see anybody fighting the flames?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was with you on that occasion, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I cannot -- it was -- I cannot recall. It was one of our teams. It would have been -- there would have been two other Americans and at least one interpreter-translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's one instance. Do you recall any other instance in 1998 where you were out in the field and saw PJP engaged in operations?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I saw PJP in the field on many occasions, but the occasion I just recounted is the only occasion in which I saw what appeared to be PJP in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to that individual sighting, were you informed or aware of other operations in 1998 by the PJP or the police, from your staff?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That -- we reported what we -- what our mission saw of this kind of activity, unfortunately very, very regularly, during the period from my arrival until the end of September of 1998. At that point, as I recall, such -- there appeared to have been a stand-down on the part of the Serbian security forces. Let me add here, for the Court, that the reports that we submitted and reports that the EU KDOM submitted would contain this information and those reports are publicly available. We ran an unclassified operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Byrnes, you said that this happened, I think, on a -- you said very regularly you saw this kind of activity. What do you mean by very regularly? Is that once a week, once a day?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Very regularly in that period, late August and September 1998, was virtually every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it always the police or only the police?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My missions reported if -- as I recall, my missions reported that this only the police were involved. Our people on the ground, who saw, particularly the consequences, the burning of villages, the destruction of crops, the killing of farm animals, that sort of thing, only reported seeing Serbian police in the area. Our clear impression, and I stress it, our clear impression was the VJ was not involved in this kind of activity during - let me add - during the time which I'm describing which is late August and all of September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After that, did there come a time where you began to see VJ in the field in some manner, involved in this kind of activity?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I personally never saw VJ involved in this sort of activity; however, I don't recall that any of my teams ever reported VJ involvement in that kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if your teams ever saw or reported any evidence of use of heavy weapons like artillery or tanks, shell fire, of that kind?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. To your knowledge, did the MUP have that kind of equipment?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the Serbian police did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the Albanian KLA have that kind of equipment?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: You're talking -- sir, you're talking about heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Heavy artillery or tanks?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the KLA did not possess such equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. These activities that you observed personally and the ones being observed by your team, did you bring these to the attention of any of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That was my job, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us how often you did that and by what means you did it?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I brought this to the attention of particularly General Lukic, who was my understanding was in charge of the Serbian police in Kosovo. I brought such information, such reports, to General Lukic's attention whenever we had this information. Sometimes I would make phone calls to him. He was -- he was very accessible. I had his cell phone number, I had his office number, and I would use it if it was necessary. As I said earlier, we often met, and I mean often during this period, often, every day. There were times when I saw him twice, three times a day because of some problem. Yes, I brought it to his attention. And on a couple of occasions, I brought it to Mr. Odalovic's attention. I brought such things to Mr. Odalovic's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you bring it to the attention of any other Serb authorities or was it only those two?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My recollection, sir, only those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not clear to me what it is we are talking about here, what it is that you're saying was brought to Mr. Lukic's attention. Can you help me on that? I know it's the use of heavy weaponry; but in conflict situations, you inevitably get the use of heavy weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm addressing is something broader, and perhaps I'm not answering your questions correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understood it to be something broader, too, but please tell us what your understanding was?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that whenever we had reports from our missions in the field of the burning of villages, destruction of personal property, the -- on some instances the surrounding of Albanian civilians and the efforts, clear efforts to intimidate Albanian civilians, or we would bring such -- I would bring such information to General Lukic's attention. Is that -- Your Honour, does that make things clearer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My misunderstanding. That is much clearer. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So to be clear, Mr. Byrnes, it was not just instances of the use of heavy artillery or heavy fire power that you were reporting, you were also reporting instances where your people saw burning of villages and burning of crops?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did your people in the field also see what was happening to the Albanian villagers in those villages?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Very simply, what we saw on, unfortunately too regular a basis, was that Albanian villagers were being driven from their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you reported that to General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the response when you provided this kind of information to him? What did he say or do?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Lukic -- as I recall, General Lukic's response was generally that either this was not happening, or in some instances he acknowledged that it was happening but it was in response to attacks from those villages by KLA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you report to him the specific event that you had seen yourself?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did he deny that one happened?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Sir, I simply do not remember what his response was, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Among the events that you reported to him, do you recall speaking to him about a specific event in connection with a sweep that the MUP had done in September 1998 near the Pec area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. I recall several occasions on which we discussed ongoing operations in the Pec area in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what was happening with the civilians in that area during that operation? Or during and after that operation?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: If I -- yes, I do, and if I may provide some background?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I unfortunately do not remember the exact dates but I do remember that it was in the September time frame. The Serbian police had launched an operation against a number of villages to the southeast of Pec, that they believed harboured KLA forces. And in the course of those operations, they drove from the villages those -- its residents, their residents. The international press got wind of the operation and provided coverage of it, which apparently embarrassed Belgrade. The international press focused particularly on the large number of displaced Albanians who were forced with their families to live in the woods and fields and this sort of thing. In response, the MUP sent forces to the area where these people were gathered and effectively herded them home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you complain about this to General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We did indeed. We complained about the way it was done. Many of these people -- they were terrified. We had several teams, not one team, we had several teams on the site and reported that unnecessary force was being used by the police against some of the displaced Albanians. The Albanians were terrified. They had no idea what was going to happen to them, particularly if they were being herded on to MUP buses. And we photographed much of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What would you say to the question about but weren't the police trying to return the people to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That was General Lukic's response; this was a humanitarian operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But your complaint had to do with?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Our complaint had to do with the use of force against these people and the way -- basically, the way it was being done. It was being -- fundamentally this was being done against their will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was his response to that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: This was a humanitarian operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the events leading up to the creation of the KVM. Could we bring up Exhibit P658? Mr. Byrnes on your screen in a minute I hope you'll have a document. I think this is sometimes referred to as the Geremek/Jovanovic agreement, or Branislav/Geremek agreement, dated the 16th of October 1998. Can you see that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen it before, or are you familiar with its contents, substance?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And is this the document that first set forth the establishment of KVM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Subsequent to this agreement, did you participate in negotiations at the White Palace in Belgrade on the 24th and 25th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you come to be a participant in those discussions?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I was present as part of the international delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who had set it up or arranged it?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Set up the talks?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I believe General Clark had set them up with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you get invited, Mr. Byrnes? Who invited you?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: As I recall, Ambassador Holbrooke and General Clark invited me to be there because they wanted somebody in the delegation who had had some expertise on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall how many participants there were at this meeting, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What I -- I can't give you an exact number but there were quite a few people around the table. I would guess we must have had 20 people around that table.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Twenty total or 20 on your side?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I would say 20 total.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall who some of the participants were? First of all on the Serb side, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Well, in the Plenary, there were discussions on two issues, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: One dealt with the VJ's role and responsibilities and the size of its presence, I recall, in Kosovo, as a result of the Geremek/Jovanovic agreement. The second set of talks dealt with the role and presence and responsibilities of the Serbian police. When the participants in both of these sets of talks met in Plenary, we must have had 30 to 40 people. Now, to try to answer your question, on our -- on the international side, General Clark was present; a German general, General Naumann, who I believe was chairman of the NATO military committee, was present; I was -- I was present; General Clark had several aides present; General Naumann had at least an aide present. On the Serbian side, the Plenary -- I recall the Plenary was chaired by President Milutinovic, but my memory may be playing tricks on me. The people -- the people I remember being present on the Serbian side were General Perisic; General Dmitrijevic; I believe his name was; then General Djordjevic; General Stefanovic; and General Lukic. I have a very distinct memories of their being present. There were others but I either didn't meet them or I can't remember their names. They were the principals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the Plenary Session where everybody attended, then did you break into smaller groups?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what group did you go off with?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Clark asked me to sit on the group that dealt with the police, the police responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who else was in the police group from your side, the international side?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: There were several. The only one I really remember was General Naumann. There were a couple of -- there were a couple of US military officers from General Clark's staff. I think Colonel Atkins was one of them, but my memory is blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And on the Serb side, who attended the police discussions?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Djordjevic chaired for the Serbian side. General Stevantovic and General Lukic were present. There were several other officers, but I -- I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the discussions, did Djordjevic act independently or did he ever consult, go out of the room, or go call someone to consult?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I recall that General Djordjevic left the talks on a number of occasions to -- we understood he was making phone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who he was talking to?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a good time for our first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Probably would, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Byrnes, we have to break at certain intervals for various reasons and now is one of these occasions. We will break for about 20 minutes so we'll resume about five minutes past 4.00; meanwhile, could you go with the Court usher? He will show you where to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, when we broke, you had -- we had just talked about how you'd gone off with the group to discuss the police matters. How long did it take your group to reach an agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the sticking point for an agreement with the MUP, if there was one in particular?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What I vaguely remember is sticking points had basically to deal with definition of terms; what constituted check-points, what constituted observation points, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you did eventually reach an agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we show the witness Exhibit P394? This is in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, I'll ask if you recognise what's about to come up on your screen; not that one. I hope there is another one on the way. That's the B/C/S and if we could have the English for you. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It's the document that was worked out during that one long day and night of talks in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could scroll to the bottom or shrink to include the signatures on the English version, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Djordjevic signed for the other side?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you come to be the signer for the international side on this particular agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I believe that General Naumann, who actually negotiated the agreement, asked me to sign it, and I think he did so because General Naumann lived and worked in Brussels and I lived and worked in Pristina. He felt that it made more sense to have a man who was there and could be in a firsthand position to observe implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. After you finally reached an agreement and signed it, what did your group do next?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I believe that we went back into a Plenary, after which we went to, I believe, it was the White Palace and President Milosevic hosted what we Americans would call a brunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And were you aware whether there had been an agreement reached on the military side of the discussions?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who had participated for the internationals on that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Clark had, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the Serbian side of the military negotiations, do you know who participated?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Perisic and others but I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mention I think before who the participants were, and I think you said earlier that President Milutinovic was there. Was Mr. Sainovic present?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I don't recall Mr. Sainovic being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we show you the next exhibit? I see an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. When someone is being asked whether he was present, the proper question to be put is who was present at the meeting; and then if the witness cannot remember any one in particular, a name can be introduced. Otherwise, it is a leading question, or perhaps Mr. Hannis can ask whether I was present and I will have no objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the context of a meeting where there were perhaps 30 people present, and in the context where it's not a game show memory test, there seems to us to be nothing wrong with asking the simple straightforward question, "Was Mr. X there or not?" That is not, in this context, what we would see to be a leading question and, therefore, we will repel the objection and allow Mr. Hannis to proceed in that way. It's already passed of course in relation to this particular part; but unless we are in a situation where there is a genuine issue over the recollection of the witness, that type of question does not seem unreasonable to any of us, especially when that's confirmed by the reasonable approach taken by the witness who says he doesn't recall. So please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Byrnes, I'd like to show you Exhibit P395. This is entitled, "Record of meeting in Belgrade, 25 October, 1998." It will be up on your screen in a minute. Let me ask you, while it's coming up, did you have occasion to see other documents that had been signed or created on that occasion, other than the one you signed yourself?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this one that's on the screen now? And we can scroll do you know if you need to see the top of it?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd like to see. To be perfectly frank, I don't remember seeing this. I probably did but it's basically a protocolary document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we go to page 3 of this document of this exhibit at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll ask you to take a look at that, and ask if you had seen that portion of this document before or are familiar with the substance of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it and I'm familiar with the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this sets forth some direction about what the VJ is supposed to do under this agreement. Were you familiar with that resolution?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have occasion then after these October agreements to be involved in monitoring or verifying whether or not that provision was being complied with?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain a little bit for the Court about this provision and what area this covered in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, by way of background, what this element of the agreement was intended to do was, as it says, was get the VJ out of the field and back into garrison. The underlying part of the underlying hope was that this would permit or encourage Albanian displaced persons which our reporting indicated, not only our reporting but that of International Red Cross elements and UNHCR elements present in the field, indicated the number of displaced persons was in the hundreds of thousands, perhaps 250.000. I don't remember the exact figure but it was quite substantial. It was great concern on the part of the international community about what would happen to these people. As they camped out on the hills, what would happen to these people during the winter. So this was in part to encourage -- to change the, if you will, the environment there and encourage -- in the hope that people would return home. Obviously, it was also intended to reduce the -- reduce the possibility of further -- further conflict. As paragraph 5 lays out, the -- General Clark and General Naumann understood that Belgrade had certain imperatives, Kosovo was part of Serbia, and they were -- there were several important lines, strategic lines of communication through the province, and Belgrade needed to protect those. Therefore, the VJ was -- it was agreed that the VJ would be permitted to station, if you will, deploy, company-sized units, including armour, as I recall, to protect -- to three different positions to protect these strategic routes. If you look at paragraph 5 and look at a map, you'll see that's precisely what General Naumann and General Clark, in their negotiations with General Perisic and others, agreed to do. I hope that's answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is. Can I ask you a follow-up question, Mr. Byrnes? Is there some significance to lines of communication that are not included in this list, if you understand? And in particular, I'm talking about the route from Pristina through Podujevo into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. The lines of communication set out in paragraph 5, A, B and C, are lines of communication inside Kosovo from -- basically, from the capital of Kosovo, Pristina, to the other major cities which were of strategic importance to Belgrade and of course to the Serbian security forces. There was one other major and strategic line of communication and that ran from Pristina north to the border, the Kosovo-Serbian border near a place, a small city named Podujevo. That two-lane asphalt highway then ran to Nis, which was the headquarters of the Yugoslav army, to which the Pristina corps was subordinate, and at Nis it connected with a major four-lane highway that ran from Nis to Belgrade. This was -- there was also a parallel train line to the highway, and it was on this highway that commercial and, of course, military traffic would move. There weren't really any other major strategic routes running from Kosovo into Serbia proper, and, therefore, maintaining control of -- and security of shall we say the Pristina-Podujevo-Nis road was of paramount concern to Belgrade and, of course, to the VJ and the Serbian police leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So given its importance, do you have an understanding of why it was not included among the three communication lines that the VJ was permitted to deploy upon under the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I do not know the answer to the question. I did not participate in this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Subsequent to this agreement, and I guess before we move on, the first page of it, as you indicated, was some sort of what you described as a protocol page, but it reflects Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic having been present. Given that, does that refresh your memory of whether Mr. Sainovic was there or not, or you still don't recollect?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I do not recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, subsequent to this agreement, in December, do you recall if there was an incident revolving around Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with the terms of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: With the terms of what agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The agreement we were just looking at about where the VJ could deploy, the three companies that were allowed to be outside the garrison.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. Our understanding was that deployment of a VJ, PJP battle group to the Podujevo area from the Marshal Tito barracks in Pristina was a violation of the agreement that I see on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall how that came to your attention?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We saw the -- we saw the units being deployed, and we and KVM followed these units to their place of redeployment near -- east of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in your -- in your view, this was in violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: In my view, and in view of Ambassador Walker, chief of the KVM mission, it was a violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally or did KDOM or KVM bring this to the attention of any of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I did not bring it to their attention personally because that was no longer my responsibility. Ambassador Walker, as head of KVM, was the principal international official. By the terms of the agreement, KVM -- it was KVM's responsibility to deal with the Serbian authorities on this -- on the agreements across the board. Ambassador Walker or certainly his operations chief, General Drewienkiewicz brought this to the attention of the appropriate authorities in Pristina. That I know there was a lot of discussion about this because this was a matter of considerable concern. We considered it very serious violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know to whom attention it was brought?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I was not present. I know I was told. I would -- for the record, let me say it was brought to the attention of the appropriate Serbian authorities in Pristina. I assume that was General Pavkovic and General Lukic because PJP units were involved in this, but I was not present at those meetings and I, therefore, cannot confirm in honesty that these were the people Walker or Drewienkiewicz -- I would add there was also one other senior Serbian official who was a General Loncar that I know Drewienkiewicz met with regularly on this kind of thing. It may have been brought to Loncar's question, but an honest answer to your question is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what the response was?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The response was that this was an exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the significance of labelling it or calling it an exercise, in terms of whether or not it's a violation of the agreement, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I can only speculate as somebody who has done a lot of political analysis in the course of their career. I can offer you what my own judgement would be, but I don't know whether that's appropriate in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the Court will allow it, I would be interested in hearing it based on your experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is perhaps a bit narrower, though, than simply looking for your analysis of what might have been behind that. The question is confined to the context of the agreement. What was the significance of labelling it or calling it an exercise, in terms of whether or not it's a violation of the agreement? Now, are you thinking of an answer that relates specifically to this agreement and based on your understanding of the use of the expression "exercise" and the way in which the agreement was reached, or are you talking about or thinking about some general political theory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm even more confused now. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you see, you started your answer by saying I can only speculate, as someone who has done a lot of political analysis in the course of their career. Now, that suggests you were going to give us your views based on some sort of political analytical experience but not necessarily specifically related to this agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- I was not present at the meetings in which this was discussed by Walker and Drewienkiewicz or the other members of their staff. I personally, as I said earlier, I personally considered this a violation of the agreement. My personal assessment at the time, and it holds still, is to call it an exercise was simply an excuse so that it was -- it was a way of rejecting the OSCE contention that this was a violation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I think that Mr. Hannis's question was really whether, if this was a genuine exercise, that would somehow or other be permitted by the agreement. Is that the question, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, it may be interpreted as not a genuine exercise. That's one matter. Let's assume it was. Would it be permitted by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without, sir, without looking at the agreement, I don't -- my recollection of the agreement is not so precise that I can answer that question directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the sort of thing I understood he was asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two matters I'd like to ask you myself. The size of the battle group that you referred to, was it bigger or similar to what was permitted under the agreement in the other three areas or three routes, communication routes, that could be protected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my recollection was it was similar in size to the other three, the other three company size groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, secondly, am I right in thinking that your description of the fourth route that doesn't appear here is in line with the location of this particular exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.
