utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the battle group that deployed on this occasion in the area of Podujevo include armour elements?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there any conflict or fire-fight between the Serb authorities and KLA on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, there was subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let me move on to something else. The KVM, when did it first begin to set up in Kosovo, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The advance elements, as I recall, arrived in very early November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was the transition intended to be accomplished or -- and in actuality how did it take place between moving from having these three KDOMs - US, EU, and Russian - into having one KVM? Can you describe that process?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We -- the KDOMs were to be generally absorbed by the new OSCE KVM mission. The KDOMs were basically to become the core of the new KVM mission which was going to be considerably larger than the three KDOMs combined. So while the three KDOMs were to be the core, a large number of additional personnel and vehicles and that sort of thing were going to be brought into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during this transitional period, did you, the KDOMs, sort of retain responsibility and in actuality were you the primary observers during that transitional period?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did that eventually take place? Did the KVM eventually absorb all the KDOMs?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. KVM eventually absorbed most of the personnel and resources of the three KDOM elements, three national KDOM elements. However, the European Union and the United States decided to retain small, if you will, representation in Pristina, and so a limited number of staff and vehicles were kept out of the KVM organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what the reason for that was?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I can only -- I can only speak to the American decision, and that was made because our ambassador of Macedonia was also the special envoy for Kosovo and was engaged in intensive negotiations in Kosovo with the then Kosovo Albanian president, Rugova, and eventually with the -- with representatives of the KLA. Washington felt it would be inappropriate to task an international organisation, the OSCE, with supporting a multilateral -- a separate multilateral diplomatic operation or mission that -- that inherent in that was even potential conflict of interest. And I should add here that the European Union had a special envoy for Kosovo, Ambassador Wolfgang Petric. He was the Austrian ambassador to Belgrade at the time. Petric and our ambassador, Christopher Hill, worked very closely together on this. It was a partnership between the United States and the European Union. Certainly Washington felt, as I said earlier, that it would be inappropriate to ask a very large international organisation to support this diplomacy. That was not their mission. So we were a very small number. A very small bit of our mission was retained to support Ambassador Hill's mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you were part of that remaining contingent?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And let me add, just for general knowledge, our mission was also tasked to provide any support necessary that we were able to provide to Ambassador Walker and his mission, and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what sorts of things, then, did you do after -- after this -- after KVM was set up and you were now remaining as this much smaller contingent to support Ambassador Hill's efforts? Did you continue to go out in the field and watch what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We went down from probably 300 officers to about 15 by mid-January of 1999. We had four or five armoured vehicles. We ran missions in coordination with KVM into areas that seemed to be hot, and we provided unclassified reporting to Washington and to Brussels and to our mission in Belgrade, on the general situation on the ground, on the humanitarian situation, and that sort of thing. That's what we did on a daily basis. Secondly, as I said earlier, we supported Ambassador Hill; and on occasion with the EU KDOM, we supported the visits of Ambassador Petric to Kosovo. And by support, I mean we would arrange meetings for them, particularly with the KLA in the field. We would provide transportation for them. We would provide interpreter services. I spent a lot of time delivering messages from Ambassador Hill in Skopje to various KLA leaders and even to President Rugova's entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the sort of thing you continued to do up until the NATO bombing started?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you leave Kosovo before the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I left Kosovo probably about -- it's sometime in late February, I would say around the 25th, 26th of February. All the EU KDOM and US KDOM were pulled out at that point. I had been at Rambouillet and I had been at Paris. When we came back from Paris, which was the second part of the Rambouillet conference, which failed to secure an agreement between both parties, what was left of KDOM was redeployed from Pristina to Skopje. And we would run missions from Skopje into Kosovo primarily to meet with Albanian and both Rugova's group and the KLA leadership, to support what was left of diplomacy, in an effort to head off a conflict but we were out of there otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After KVM had become fully set up and you were the smaller contingent, how did you interact and coordinate with them in terms of what you were going to do each day?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It was a transition process. We had much, much more contact with KVM at the beginning. We needed to put them in touch with our contacts both on the Albanian side and on the Serbian side, contacts in Pristina, contacts in the field. We had to transfer vehicles and equipment to them from our operations. We took them to our meetings; for example, I used to take a couple of KVM officers to the daily meetings we had with General Lukic, which were established after the Jovanovic/Geremek agreement was signed. And, of course, in the early stages, we worked very hard to coordinate missions into the field because the resources were still short, and there were many, many potential points of conflict. As we became quite -- we in the U.K. Dom became quite small, such coordination became less necessary, and as I recall we did it often just by radio. It was -- in fact, it was usually the case of a KVM headquarters calling us saying, Something is going on some place. Do you have anybody out there that can check? We don't. So if we had somebody in the neighbourhood, we would run them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, was the second stage of Rambouillet not later than the 25th or 26th of February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought it wound up -- it wound up before March. That's my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My memory, Your Honour, is it wound up before March. I don't have a precise date in front of me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did you pull out following the failure of these talks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Byrnes, being in Rambouillet and then in Paris. Had you pull out of Kosovo before the Paris talks?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. We pulled out of Kosovo once before, in the middle of October of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What was that about? You pulled out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's because, I think, Mr. Hannis, that I certainly when I was talking about the second stage of Rambouillet, was speaking of what you've referred to as Paris, and I think Mr. Byrnes's answer is that it was following the final failure of the efforts to resolve the matter, so that's the second stage in Paris that the mission pulled out. You then asked the question if they had pulled out before, and now you've heard that on one prefer occasion in October, which may or may not have any relevance to what we are discussing, there was a pullout.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct? Is that a correct summary of the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us then that you went back into Kosovo in July 1999, after the conflict ended?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I arrived back in Kosovo mid-June, after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes. I don't have any other questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Now, I understand that the letter of 12th April has now been relayed to the United States government representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The correct procedure for these communications, and the same applies to requests that might ultimately lead to applications under Rule 54 bis, is that the parties themselves should be submitting these documents directly to the government in question. We can quite understand your anxiety to make is sure that we are informed and to lodge copies in some form here, probably by filing them with the Registry, but it will cause delay and on occasions confusion if the communication is not, in fact, sent direct to the government, and that seems to be what's happened here, that there was delay at least and possibly a measure of confusion caused by the procedure adopted. However, we are beyond that stage now and want to look at reality. Now, a quick glance at these five categories on which authority is sought to cross-examine suggests to me that they will not all be easily resolved. Can you assist, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I had a brief discussion with Ms. Manning and Ms. Schildge. I would also indicate, Your Honour, that I would have an objection as to relevance and foundation for some of these topics because, unless there is some basis for this witness being asked questions about those matters, I would say it's just a fishing expedition and I would oppose it, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me letters for these, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, B, C, D, and E. I'm okay with A. Your Honour, the witness would like to have a short break and step out to the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly. We can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll be right back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- we can manage without you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be best if we were to ask the witness just to remain outside the room briefly while we deal with what you say about matters B to E. Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Hannis raises the question of relevance and foundation in relation to items B to E. It's easy to see why he raises the matter, and I think for us to explore this properly would require to you address it in more detail first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I'm a little surprised insofar as Mr. Hannis in his questioning elicited information relating to item B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, item D?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Item B. We just had information at page 48 on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there may be a difference between what is said in D and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: B, Your Honour, B as in boy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, in B?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what do you say in B is not covered by A?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, A was meant to talk about official discussions and B was meant to be informal or private messages. I don't know to what extent the messages that the witness talked about in direct were official contact or private contact, giving instructions on the KLA for how they should act and giving the KLA information about how NATO was prepared to act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that that door has been opened in any event by the questions in examination-in-chief, which Mr. Hannis no doubt contends they fall within A any way, why is A not sufficient for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be sufficient for the purposes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You think it will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Can we deal then with C?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That one was to follow-up on some information we had, and we just wanted ask some basic questions. I didn't expect I was going to elicit much information relative to this and, in fact, don't have many questions prepared relative to this topic. We just want to find out the extent to which that particular US agency was involved in Kosovo and whether it had people on the ground in Kosovo, particularly with respect to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The relevance of that to the issues in the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it would establish that perhaps some of the international observers that were on the ground that were reporting had a different agenda or motive. You will recall we have had evidence from some of the -- that came in through some of the KVM witnesses about some of the differences of opinion among some of the various staff members of the KVM and in particular some allegations of misreporting, based upon different allegiances in particular to members of the KVM this were of the American nationality and had been former US KDOM personnel. So that might help bring the truth to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the area of the accuracy of the reporting of the US KDOM staff is plainly an issue that you can explore, and putting the name of the Central Intelligence Agency into your request adds something that doesn't on the face of it have a relevance to issues in the trial. The issue is the accuracy of how matters are dealt with. Nationality may have something to do with it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Affiliation to that agency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- how do you see references to that agency as helping.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We also had testimony from one witness - off the top of my head, I can't remember - who indicated that in his opinion there was, in Rambouillet and elsewhere, efforts by the American administration to get rid of the Milosevic regime through any means possible, basically that the peaceful efforts were sabotaged and the -- that particular agency could be said to be dealing with those type of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, there would be very minimal examination on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as D is concerned, you've heard more of Mr. Byrnes's involvement in diplomatic and politically diplomatic matters than you were privy to before today, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And D, I take it, would be restricted to relevant service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Service that might be relevant to the issues that we are dealing with today --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To the Balkans, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- rather than his full personal dossier. Can it be read subject to that qualification?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what about E?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: E is more of a specific development of what was set forth in C, so I think E and C could be combined to further specify precisely the matters that would be sought for explanation, if the witness even knows. If he doesn't know, it's going to be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds as though you don't have a foundation for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have had one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, since this witness was the head of the US mission, and we've had at least one witness who was deeply involved in the negotiation process point the finger at the US administration and the US officials for being the ones to try and sabotage the talks, I don't know who else I should be asking the question to. This witness is here. If he knows, he knows; if he doesn't, then I don't go any further with the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there are two questions really. One is did he do anything to destabilise the government of Milosevic, and the second question is does he know of anyone else who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does he personally know?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now is there anything else you want to say on any of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if D and E are restricted in the way suggested, do you maintain that there is no relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but with not as much vigour. The reason is, Your Honour, I just have a general dissatisfaction with that kind of questioning without some firm basis of some good faith foundation for asking the question and the fact that there may have been some vague allegation about CIA or efforts to destabilise. I don't think it's fair to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you about D and E at the moment. I'm trying to steer clear of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- vague references to -- not vague references, but references to agencies whose role we are unlikely to be able to identify specifically in the course of a trial such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I thought were you asking about C and E because Mr. Ivetic had linked them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I'm suggesting in relation to D, you've already raised a number of matters about the service of Mr. Byrnes, all relevant to the case; and if cross-examination is raised, it seems to me not unreasonable. I know that that's a matter, material that they weren't familiar with, but he certainly had no difficulty in dealing with your questions. And as far as E is concerned, the question is -- and you'll understand why this question arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is related to how well the US KDOM and indeed the EU KDOM did merge into KVM and the extent to which they had separate roles, and we've heard clearer indication today than before of what happened and the reason for it happening. So there seem to be areas there that might be explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that -- and B really disappears because A is wide enough to cover the issue subject obviously to control of the questions, and that takes us back to C as being one on which I think we would have to deliberate before we give you an indication of how we see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't need anything from me on C at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, this discussion has helped to focus attention on what may be the most important aspects of this for you, and I think on certain elements of the request, which are in terms that would be very unlikely to be granted, we can do no more at this stage than endeavour to facilitate resolution of this, and we hope we've done that by allowing parties to exchange more fully their views on the matter. You may wish to consider, in the light of that, amending your request. It's a matter for you. If you decide not to, then that, we understand, is the position you take, and the US government would have to take a decision on the terms of the letter as it stands. On the other hand, if you feel that this discussion has assisted in focusing issues more specifically and more helpfully, then you might wish to amend the letter. We believe that to you. The trouble is you don't have much time, if you want to have it dealt with and Mr. Byrnes cross-examined, if that's permitted, at this time. I don't know what his arrangements are because it looks as though we might have some time on our hands and may be able to allow an adjournment for that without necessarily requiring to bring him back at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That may be possible, Your Honour. We would have to check with him, but I should advise I saw my by an e-mail that we are now scheduled to sit in the morning tomorrow instead of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only if it's going to be convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of seeking some information from the US tonight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The reason for that was that my general or our general understanding is that parties prefer mornings to afternoons and because of events this morning, then the mornings are available this week. But if you wish to adhere to the afternoon, then we shall. It's of no particular importance to us. If you think, Mr. Hannis, that tomorrow afternoon, if we sit tomorrow afternoon, that's going to help, then we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I'm getting a yes from over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we will do that. It's unlikely that. It is unlikely that the cross-examination will take the whole of the day any way, so it's not likely to be a late finish. But Mr. Ivetic, can we ask you to take a fairly quick decision, not to tell us, but a quick decision on what you intend to do, and to communicate one way or the other, but do not leave it unsaid, what your position is before we close tonight, hopefully, so that there is some time at least for this to be considered by the US government? We can now have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Byrnes. We did have an issue to try to resolve, and we have made progress on it. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll follow the indictment, and I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour, but I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, it is not my intention to bother you, but I will try to be as brief as possible. I appear on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. My name is Toma Fila. I will pose a few questions but if you cannot recall certain things, please tell us so. The first thing I'm interested in is this: You mentioned Veljko Odalovic. In this case, he will be brought by our Defence. I would like to hear your opinion as to his credibility. In your view, was he cooperative? Did you cooperate with him well? And what would be your general assessment of that person, since he is an important witness for us?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Toma -- Mr. Fila, Veljko Odalovic was very cooperative. I felt that we had a very good working relationship. He was always accessible to me and to the other KDOMs, and there were several occasions on which I went to him with very serious problems in the field and asked for his help in getting a positive resolution to them. And in my memory, on every -- in my memory, on every single of these occasions, he was cooperative and responsive; and on at least several instances, at least one instance in particular I recall, he succeeded in getting -- in meeting my request, in getting the problem resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering one of Mr. Hannis's questions, you said that you were not informed as to the precise role of Sainovic. Were you told this by His Excellency Mr. Miles or maybe Mr. Sainovic spoke of his role? But I failed to understand, did you have any reliable information as to the scope of his authority? But before you answer, I wanted to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a Defence document, 2D8, and it keeps coming back, Your Honours. I'm fed up with it but there is nothing else to do. Could we please have that on the screen? When we are done with the trial, Your Honours, I will be -- I will still be dreaming of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is a document from the government of Yugoslavia, in which we can see that pursuant to a decision by the Yugoslav government, the federal commission for the cooperation with the OSCE mission was formed. The president of the commission - now you can see it before you - was the vice prime minister, Mr. Sainovic. The decision was signed by Momir Bulatovic, who was the president of the federal government. Could you please read items 2 and 3 -- actually, item 2? There, you can see the scope of Mr. Sainovic's authority given to him by the Yugoslav government. Further down, you see the members of the commission; Mr. Zivadin Jovanovic, Pavle Bulatovic, then the Ministers of Defence and Foreign Affairs, and so on and so forth. You will see that these are the top officials of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. My question is this: Based on what you can see here, when you met Sainovic and when you had a chance to talk to him, was he conducting his duties? Was he going about his duties, the way as was envisaged by this document and signed by the president of the commission --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: As the president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. The following thing I wanted to ask you is this: We have heard several witnesses here; for example, Mr. Philips, who confirmed something that we found in certain documents but they are under seal; therefore, I won't be specific here. He said that you felt safe in Kosovo when in the presence of the MUP and the VJ and that you did not request any additional security. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, if Mr. Fila is going to be asking about things that are in Mr. Philip's notes, those are under seal and the substance, if we are going to discuss them, we should discuss in closed session, because that was the order pursuant to our request for non-disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we don't understand each other. It wasn't in Mr. Philip's notes, but rather in some other notes. I am trying to stay out of private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The fact remains, Mr. Fila, that we are talking about material which is under seal. You recognise that, so I presume you're being careful to avoid disclosing anything publicly that is meant to be protected. So proceed on that basis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Did you feel safe in the presence of the police and the army, and did you need any additional security? It is a simple question.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The answer is yes, da.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question is this: In those meetings, and based on your experience during your stay there, did you see Mr. Sainovic's role as being of importance because, first and foremost, he was an official who cooperated with you, and did you know what the system of decision making was in place at the time within the federal government? Did you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, that's compound. I'm not sure which of three questions he wants to have answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time for a break, I think. Mr. Fila can sort out the order in which he wishes these various questions answered during that break. This time, for half an hour, Mr. Byrnes, so we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, what do you know exactly about the functioning of the Yugoslav state and government? Do you know what the decision system looked like within the federal government and the government of Serbia? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the extent of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, not as great as yours but I think I had a basic fundamental understanding of the basic decision making process, as certainly as it was described on paper; you know, the organisation chart, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Would you agree with me if I said that Sainovic, in your meetings with you, was cooperative, that he did not deliver propaganda or tirades of sorts?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with you completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me if I said that Sainovic thought that the situation in Kosovo should have been resolved by political means providing for some sort of an autonomy for the province, which would be established through negotiations with the mediation of the international community?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, yes, I would agree with that; and if I may, let me add that he and I had several discussions, general discussions, about this issue. My clear impression, based on those discussions, was that he, as a practical politician, sought to find a mutually acceptable political solution to this problem and he was working in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would that include his attempt, when he asked you to try and organise a meeting with the KLA leadership in Dragovlja, if you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did that show a clear intention on his part to negotiate with the KLA so as to achieve the goals we've mentioned a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I, Mr. Fila, understood his request as, in fact, an initiative on his part to reach out to the KLA leadership in an effort to find some sort of a solution; and if I may, I'd like to add that my recollection is that his -- his question or request, if you will, about whether such a meeting would be possible, whether I could arrange it, whether US government could arrange it, whether he would be secure in an area that was in fact controlled by the KLA, my recollection is that conversation occurred after the successful release of the eight VJ soldiers taken by the KLA in January and the subsequent release of nine KLA captured, I think, in December by the VJ when they tried to cross the border from Albania into Kosovo. I think, in the conversation, Mr. Sainovic even said something to the effect that we had been successful in arranging this sort of -- this sort of agreement, this sort of deal, if you will, perhaps we could use that as a basis and expand it into something that had a broader political consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For example, to continue with prisoner exchanges, and he saw that as an opportunity to calm the situation down and try to pave the way to come up with a peaceful solution. Would you agree with me if I said that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That I agree, and he actually posed the issue in those terms, as you would say in Serbian, [B/C/S spoken]. He saw this as perhaps prisoner exchanges could lead eventually to something bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: The meeting he requested at Dragovlja, was this on his own initiative, in your view?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I don't know the answer to that, and I, frankly, many times posed the same question to myself. Was Mr. Sainovic, in this particular regard, acting on his own or was he not? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us go to Rambouillet for a moment. At Rambouillet, were you under the impression that Sainovic's approach was a flexible and a constructive one, but that the work of the delegation was limited by something back in Belgrade? How would you describe Sainovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: First, to be absolutely clear, at the Rambouillet conference, I was only present for the first couple of days. I was then sent back to Kosovo, and I had no contact with Mr. Sainovic at Rambouillet per se that I can remember. At the second stage of those talks, the ones that took place in Paris, I was present, and I did have a fair amount of contact -- I'd say some contact with Mr. Sainovic. We had several conversations. And I remember distinctly on one occasion, when I was pushing Mr. Sainovic to try to -- in order that the Serbian delegation be more flexible, my basic point I recall was telling them that -- telling him, who I knew well at that time, that the NATO threat of bombing Serbia was not a bluff, that General Clark and NATO were absolutely serious about this, and he needed to understand that. And, secondly, if it came to that, at the end of the day, Serbia was unlikely to get a better deal than what they were being offered at Rambouillet. And as somebody who knew something about Serbia, I recognised this was not a deal that was going to be welcomed by most of the Serbian population, but we were dealing with a very difficult political reality. And the options seemed either to be war and more loss of life on everybody's side or a deal that most Serbs would not like, but might preserve the peace, would reserve Kosovo's organic relationship with Serbia proper, and would return Kosovo to the autonomy that Slobodan Milosevic had stripped from it in 1989. It would return it to the autonomy that the constitution of I believe 1974 had awarded it. And I distinctly remember Mr. Sainovic sitting there thoughtfully and finally responding to my question with words something to the effect that he did not have the authority to be that flexible, that there were too many constraints on him imposed by Belgrade, and at the end of the day, there was nothing he could do in this direction, whether he wanted to or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In other words, you will agree with me that Sainovic did his very best to be flexible, he himself, that is, but that obviously he was constrained in that by the actual powers he had from Belgrade. Is that what you were actually trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What I would say is, first, I was not in Mr. Sainovic's shoes. I do not know, therefore, whether he did everything he possibly could. He told me he did. Fundamentally, I trusted that. I trusted what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Byrnes. Your Honour, this concludes our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Byrnes. I'm Norman Sepenuk, and I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic. I have very few questions for you and they are about Podujevo. You testified that according to Prosecution Exhibit 395, which was what I'll call the Clark-Naumann agreement, paragraph 5 thereof. There were three areas where the VJ was allowed to deploy forces, and the Pristina Podujevo area was not one of them; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this agreement was signed on 25 October 1998. Can you cast your mind back to October 25, 1998? Do you have any recollection as to the extent, if any, of KLA activities in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My -- I very frankly don't have very -- a very clear recollections of day-to-day activity. To be very frank, my clearest recollections are of the crises itself. What I can honestly feel I can say is that that area was a very troublesome one for KVM and for us. The KLA commander - they called it the lap zone - the lap zone commander was very aggressive, and my recollection is that he was constantly pushing the envelope, if you will. I think KVM had an outstation in Podujevo and they worked very hard to keep both sides apart and, if you will, everybody on the reservation; in other words, they worked very hard to ensure that these agreements were respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you are talking about Commander Remi, correct, the lap commander, Remi?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He was very aggressive and sort of intransigent, was he?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Commander Remi was a very aggressive and militarily very capable officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But getting back to my question: It's fair to say you don't have any particular recollection as to the extent of KLA activity, if any, during that period of October 25th, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The answer would basically be yes, I don't have any specific -- very specific recollection of KLA -- specific day-to-day KLA activity there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But I take it you do have a recollection that once these agreements were signed, I'll call them the October agreements, that Serb forces did vacate that area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And not long after they vacated that area, at least coming into December of 1998, it's also fair to say, isn't it, that the KLA just occupied the areas vacated by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The KLA occupied some areas that had been vacated by the Serb forces, particularly areas to the west. I guess it would be the north west of the Pristina-Podujevo road. Other areas they vacated, we -- I spent personally a lot of time immediately after the October agreement in the Podujevo area in an effort to persuade Remi and his commanders to pull their units back, particularly from those areas where they posed, in purely military terms, they posed a threat to the strategic Pristina-Podujevo road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So when they moved back into those areas, they did indeed pose a threat to that road, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: From a military standpoint, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I suppose from a civilian standpoint, too, wasn't it? I mean civilians had to travel along that road, too, did they not?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In addition to the threat posed to the military, their supply lines and what not, were you also aware, I assume you were, were you also aware of the fact that the KLA was essentially driving out most of the Serbian population of the area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We heard reports to that effect from the Serbian authorities, particularly from the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how about from Mr. Veljko Odalovic. I take it you had fairly frequent contact with him?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Indeed, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you ever talk to him about this rather serious problem of KLA driving out Serbs from the area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I know Mr. Odalovic and I talked at least in general terms about that general problem across Kosovo. With specific regard to the Podujevo area, what I'd like to point out that at the time, which we are discussing, in other words, early December 1998, KDOM no longer had a presence there. That was a KVM responsibility. As I pointed out earlier, KVM had an outpost in Podujevo once they patrolled the area, once they maintained contact with the Serbian community, with the Albanians, with the police, with the KLA, et cetera, so forth. Our knowledge and my personal knowledge of what was going on in that area at the time derived from KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't -- you weren't sort of on the ground there observing what was going on?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No, sir, we were not, again, at that particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But had you heard from either Mr. Odalovic or anybody else about the plight of the civilians there in Podujevo, the Podujevo area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I honestly don't have a recollection of hearing something specifically about the plight of the Serbian civilians in that area. I did hear a lot on that subject from Mr. Odalovic and from General Lukic; and also, the Serbian police provided us on a daily basis with their own reports of activity across Kosovo, and there would be information about this particular -- the question you're asking in those reports. So I was not unaware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So let me simply read one paragraph to see if I can refresh your recollection, to see if this jibes with your recollection. It's Prosecution Exhibit 414, it's dated 11 December 1998, and it's from two gentlemen who are members of the Podujevo municipal assembly; the executive committee chairman and the president. Did you know either one of those, by the way, Mr. Srevlos Beseric [phoen] and Milovin Tomic? Did you know either one of those gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. But let me just read this one brief part, just to see if it jibes with your recollection of what was going on. This is a letter again December 11, 1998 from these two gentlemen who were part of the Podujevo municipal assembly, and it was sent to a number of people. Aside from Slobodan Milosevic, it was also sent to Veljko Odalovic the chief of the Kosovo district, with whom you had fairly constant contact. It says, "They," meaning the KLA - this is on page 2, "They" -- do you ever that? "They have become so strong that in addition to marauding, literally armed to the teeth with automatic rifles, hand-held rocket launchers on their shoulders, necklaces of hand grenades, and cartridge belts and the camouflage and black uniforms of what they call their police, they come right up to the town, they encircle individual isolated Serbian houses, carry out searches, mistreat people, and make threats and give deadlines to people to move out from Podujevo municipality." Does this jibe with your recollection of part of what was going on in the Podujevo area during that period?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: A technical point: I don't see that in the letter here, but yes, it does jibe with my recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And that was on, by the way -- for the record, it was on page 2 of that letter, Exhibit 414. You mentioned black uniforms. Does that ring a bell with you, black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I saw black uniforms when I was in Kosovo. I don't know immediately in what context I was quoted mentioning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you recall that the KLA secret police wore black uniforms and can you -- can I refresh your recollection by just stating that and maybe you can tell us a little bit more about what you knew about the KLA secret police wearing these black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I recall that the KLA -- I recall being told the KLA secret police wore black uniforms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you at one time describe them, you, Mr. Byrnes, describe them as "sinister"?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the unit was commanded by a gentleman named Geci, correct, G-E-C-I?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My understanding was that unit was commanded by a man named Sabit [phoen] Geci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. And as I understand it, you described Mr. Geci as ruthless, responsible for the murder of Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are getting questions into the substance of material that is subject to the protective order. So if we are going to continue to ask questions that draw from those matters for which there is a protective order, then we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That was my last question on it, Your Honour, and that calls for a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes or no to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. So with the KLA posing a very serious threat to the military, as you've stated, and with the rather desperate and appalling situation the civilians in Podujevo, don't you think there is at least some reasonable basis to say that the actions of the VJ forces fell within that part of the Clark-Naumann agreement which allowed Serb forces, consistent with the right of self-defence, to respond adequately and proportionately to any form of terrorist activity or violation of law which could jeopardise the lives and safety of citizens and representatives of the state authorities? Isn't there really a basis for that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We recognised the right of the Serb security forces to defend themselves and their citizens, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Byrnes, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic, and I think I have one and a half questions for you basically. I think with regard to your knowledge of General Pavkovic, what you have said about him was that he was direct and professional, and at one point you referred to him as a soldier's soldier who did not get involved in lectures on Serb history or politics. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, that's a fair statement. But let me point out for the record I met General Pavkovic only once, but I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And with regard to the VJ, as you pretty much told us here today, your view of the VJ was that it conducted itself both professionally and honourably, both before and during the conflict; and, in fact, what you said about the shelling that was done with the heavy weaponry of the VJ was that it was not intended to cause casualties but more in the nature of causing harassment or fear. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's -- that's what I said for the record earlier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether I have one and a half questions, too, or is it two, perhaps, but let me ask Mr. Byrnes, or rather, let me add something to what Mr. Ackerman said, and also if we look at the notes that we got I'm really not going to use any material that would make it incumbent on us to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But Mr. Byrnes, is it correct, and you confirmed just now, that as you had quoted,, it was a fact that the army of Yugoslavia, even after the NATO air strikes began, it behaved in a decent and professional manner and that that is the information you got from the Albanians themselves, who said that the army of Yugoslavia gave them food, water, that they helped in many situations. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I received information from Kosovar Albanians who had worked for us at KDOM as interpreters, drivers, and that sorts of thing, as well as from some members of the Kosovar Albanian political elite who fled Kosovo after the conflict began, to the effect that the Yugoslav army, when they encountered them - they being the Albanian displaced persons - had treated them with respect; and in one particular instance had even intervened to save the lives of one of my interpreters and his colleague, who they thought, they thought - and I stress that - were about to be executed by apparent Serbian paramilitaries. My speaking more broadly - and I stress this is not eye witness experience; it's second, third hand - speaking more broadly, however, my general impressions are that the Yugoslav army generally behaved honourably and well, after the bombing started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes. Another question. After the agreement that we discussed here, is it also correct that as for the deployment of the army of Yugoslavia and the units of the army of Yugoslavia, was it not transparent and were there ever any problems in terms of supervising the deployment?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Let me say, before I answer that question directly, in my position as head of KDOM, we had very little responsibility, after the signing of the October agreement, to monitor specific Yugoslav military operations, activities, and particularly the deployment and redeployment of forces as directed by the October agreements. That task fell to KVM, and a British military contingent headed by General Drewienkiewicz arrived very quickly after the agreement was signed and to bring the military expertise necessary to do that, and they did it. That said, my general impression, based on what I heard from Drewienkiewicz and his colleagues, was the deployments were transparent, as you asked. Does that -- is that -- is that a clear answer to your question? I mean, I want to be sure I'm clear on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Byrnes. Thank you very much. Just an additional question: Do you know that KDOM carried out 30 verifications of the weaponry of the army of Yugoslavia without a single objection raised in the process?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I frankly don't remember the numbers, but I know that the military members of KDOM - and KDOM was made up half of US diplomats and half of US military officers - our military officers were seconded to KVM for these verification missions and what you said is what I generally remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. It was my mistake. It was American KDOM that actually carried out the inspections of these weapons. I have just one question left. It's my last question. Actually, I didn't even introduce myself to you at the very beginning, and it has to do with General Lazarevic. You mentioned that you were never in contact with General Lazarevic. Is it also correct that you stated, when you talked to the investigators, that no one ever mentioned him in your presence?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have gone through this more quickly than I anticipated. I have sent the amended request to the Prosecutor's Office and asked them to rely that to the representatives of the United States. I'm wondering at this time, since it looks like I've been rewriting my questions and culling through them and getting rid of some questions that are no longer relevant, it looks like I should be able to finish with this witness within 45 minutes to an hour. Would it be more efficient to wait until we hear the response from the US and finish with it in one fell swoop tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I think it would be better to start now and finish at 7.00 and see how you get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, my name is Dan Ivetic, and I'm one of the attorneys representing Sreten Lukic in these proceedings. Again, I would just stress that since we are speaking the same language, we need to have a pause between questions and answers and try not to overlap, and I think we can get through most of this fairly quickly. Now, first of all, sir, I'd like to take you back to the formation of the KVM and the interactions between the US KDOM and the KVM. Now, during the time period when the KDOM was standing in for the KVM, I presume that the KDOM received much information and documentation from the Serb authorities, including the Serbian MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And once the KVM mission got up and running on its feet in Kosovo, am I correct that the US KDOM provided the fledging KVM with all the information and documents at its disposal that it had received previously from the Serb authorities, including the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we have heard some testimony from various -- I shall strike that. I'm probably getting into an area that I'm not supposed to yet without a decision. Now, if I can ask you about the KVM mission in general, was it a problem with the KVM mission that it had a variety of persons who are not specifically trained for the role that they were undertaking; for instance, observers who had no police training being verifiers for the police? Do you have that knowledge of the KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I would say it's a very difficult question for me to answer. I would try to answer it by saying my personnel that we set out didn't have any special training for observing the police activities. I suppose if the KVM personnel assigned had been policemen or had prior training, perhaps they would have done a better job. I'm sorry. That's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. If I can ask you about an observation that I believe you made in your interview with the Prosecutor's Office, am I correct that your observation was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If he's going to be quoting from the interview, then we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's your intention, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It wasn't to quote but the question can be construed as a quote, so perhaps I should ask a different question so we can avoid perhaps going into close session for a very minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try again and let's see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, do you have any personal knowledge about the reputations that General Drewienkiewicz, General DZ, and William Walker, the heads of the KVM mission, had among the Serbs? That is to say, was any information communicated to you about the general attitudes of people dealing with General DZ and with Mr. Walker or Ambassador Walker?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, does this question concern their reputations before their arrival or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time period that they were assigned to part of the KVM.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I don't recall anything directly regarding the reputation of General Drewienkiewicz; in other words, if I understand the -- correctly what the Serbs thought of General Drewienkiewicz, what his reputation was among Serbs. With regard to William Walker, I had the very distinct impression that the Serbs considered him anti-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Did you have any knowledge of either the KVM or the KDOM having problems due to the quality issues with the translators that were employed, the local language translators that were employed out in the field?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I vaguely recall complaints or hearing complaints from our colleagues in KVM on occasion about, I guess, the quality of the language expertise of some of their local translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can ask you a related question: With respect to your meetings, in particular, your meetings with General Lukic, am I correct that for the most part, these meetings took place without the use of an interpreter; that is to say, you conversed in the Serbian language with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And before we move on to another topic, let me just ask you to see if I can perhaps clarify your recollection: You had testified that you met General Lukic at his office on or about the 13th of August 1998 when you were introduced by Ambassador Miles. Do you recall perhaps that the first time you met General Lukic was in fact at the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs office and that Ambassador Miles indeed was not the individual -- was not present, and that the issue upon your first meeting with General Lukic was the security of the US KDOM personnel, discussions regarding providing for the security of the US KDOM personnel? Is it possible that you were perhaps mistaken, and does this refresh your recollection as to when you first met General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It does refresh my memory. I do remember meeting General Lukic in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and I do remember that the discussion was of KDOM security. I frankly don't remember the date, but it stands to reason that that would have been one of the first meetings I had on arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while we are on the topic of the Serbian MUP, regarding the various agreements from October 1998 onwards, I believe the so-called Geremek/Jovanovic agreement, in Article 1, Section 9, sets forth that the FRY government will designate former liaison officers to work with the verification mission. Do you recall if in fact the FRY authorities, specifically the Serbian MUP, designated a former liaison officer to work with the KVM in Pristina, specifically Colonel Mijatvic, whom you mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's consistent with my recollections, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also consistent with your recollections that formal liaison officials were set up on the part of the Serbian MUP also at the local level; that is to say, at field locations based around the various SUPs or Secretariats in the Kosovo/Metohija province?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you would receive written summaries from the MUP, written daily reports from the MUP, about the situation out in the field. Am I correct that the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs continued sending such detailed reports to the US KDOM, simultaneously to sending those same to the KVM; that is to say, even though KVM was on the ground, KDOM remained apprised on a daily basis by the Serbian MUP of the situation in the field?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To be very precise, I don't know whether they were sent simultaneously, to US KDOM and KVM, but I confirm that MUP did send their daily reports to us religiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that the various MUP liaison officers maintained in daily regular contact with the liaison officers, both on the KVM side and with the US KDOM side, giving access to information and concerns?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I cannot confirm that the various MUP liaison officers maintained daily contact in the field with the -- at the SUP level with the KVM liaison officers. I simply wasn't privy to that information, and our unit was so small at that point that we could not possibly track that sort of thing. The second part of your question relates to liaison officers, MUP liaison officers with US KDOM. After KVM stood up, the only -- what I recall is the only frequent liaison we had with MUP was in Kosovo Polje itself, and it was a very cooperative relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your testimony and during your direct examination, you touched upon the PJP, and you said that these were not regular police doing traffic stops, et cetera. We had multiple witnesses, including some members or former members of the PJP, who testified that in fact they were regular police officers who would be called upon in times of need or emergency to provide supplemental or separate services, especially when dealing with emergency situations. Is -- does that refresh your recollection as to your statement that the PJP were not regular police officers; that is to say, are you aware of the fact that indeed the members of the PJP were regular police officers who were tasked when called up as part of the PJP to deal with emergent circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What you say makes sense. They clearly were members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct that you never saw any official documents at the time when you were stationed as part of the US KDOM setting forth the structure, particularly the command structure, of the Serbian MUP and the duties of the various organs of the Serbian MUP, particularly the MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I think -- I think, I'm correct in saying yes, but I would like to add, and by official documents I mean official Serbian government documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Legislation, acts, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I'm sure I've seen that stuff, whether I saw it down there or not. But I can tell you General Lukic walked us through that at one point so that we understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked about the incident that you saw in a village near Kijevo. I wasn't sure if it was Kijevo itself or another subvillage, since you could not provide any further details for it. Am I correct that you came after there had been a fierce battle between the Serb forces and the KLA in that village or area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: For the record, the village is located several kilometres south of Kijevo itself. I don't recall the name of it. I don't know whether there had been a fierce battle there or not. I told you, and I told the Court what I saw. We arrived at this village which was burning, and we saw PJP forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Had you asked for such information from anyone present; i.e., had you asked if any combat had just taken place prior -- at any time prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I would like to add that when we encountered the police in such situations, they were generally quite uncooperative and -- let me replace that word. They were quite uncommunicative.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to -- with respect to the KLA, why don't we move for a moment to the KLA. Isn't it a fact that the KLA was continually active throughout Kosovo/Metohija from August 1998 onwards, based upon your knowledge and information being on the ground there from August 1998 onwards, for the time period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that with the October accords being entered into, the provocative activities of the KLA actually increased? I'll ask that as the first question and then I have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, how do you describe -- how do you define "provocative."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's not use provocative. Let's use armed activities of the KLA increased after the signing of the October accords.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I would say that in certain sectors of Kosovo, the armed activities of the KLA seemed to increase, and the sector I have in mind, in particular mind, was Malisevo in central Kosovo in the period immediately after the signing of the October agreements. In other sectors for a time activities seemed to be reduced is what I remember, but it was reduced on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we had some evidence led through witnesses and through documents from the KVM that in fact following the signing of the October accords, the KLA was responsible for a majority of the breaches of the cease-fires. Does that comport to your recollection of the events on the ground at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What I remember was that we had problems with both sides, with respect to breaches, with respect to fire-fights, and that sort of thing. There were problems on both sides, and they were regional-specific. As I pointed out earlier, we had more problems in the Malisevo area initially. My deputy and I and the head of EU KDOM devoted an awful lot of time and energy to that sector trying to calm things down. Other sectors were quieter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that there was a significant KLA presence in the Malisevo region?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony from a Commander Zyrapi here regarding the fact that following the October accords, the KLA held more territory than it had before. Does that comport to the information you had available to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Commander Zyrapi also provided information that the KLA had plans to move into the urban centres and begin to form groups to carry out attacks within urban centres and big cities. Is that something that comports to your knowledge and recollection of events on the ground during that time period?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We at US KDOM did not have specific information indicating that would happen, but there were rumours. There was hearsay, if you will, circulating in Albanian society that that was going to happen, and we at US KDOM and our counterparts at KVM, I can confirm, were deeply concerned about that prospect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was going to ask if this was a suitable time to interrupt you, but I won't stop you if this is related to this same matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can do one more question, Your Honour. It won't hurt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the information circulating in the Albanian society, am I correct that one of the items of information that you brought to General Lukic during one of your meetings was that approximately 30.000 pieces of long arms; that is to say, long-barrelled rifles, had been transported or smuggled across the border from Albania into Kosovo and were now in the hands of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I honestly have no recollection of such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. We'll take up then I guess tomorrow if Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. The afternoon is still your preference, Mr. Hannis, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no strong preference. I don't know if the witness has a preference but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you indicated that you were more likely to have answers, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, given the time difference, I think it probably doesn't make a difference. We'll get the answer before tomorrow morning either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, depending on when I get the answer, if I get it first thing in the morning, it may impede my ability to prepare questions for it, but I can perhaps work with Mr. Hannis and get that resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's adhere to the arrangement for the afternoon in that case and resume tomorrow at 2.15, same time as today. Mr. Byrnes, overnight, it's important that you don't discuss your evidence, either what you have said already or what you might say in evidence in this case, with anyone at all. Please talk about other things. I'm sure you'll be delighted to, and there is no restriction on what you can talk about.
